 Jonathan Nolan is one of the most-acclaimed science-fiction writers working today. After collaborating with his brother Christopher Nolan on iconic films like Memento , The Dark Knight , and Interstellar , the youngest Nolan sibling has reshaped big-budget sci-fi TV with acclaimed works like Westworld and Fallout . Yet before he entered prestige television, he put a sci-fi spin on a network procedural that has aged remarkably well since it debuted 15 years ago.

 In 2011, Jonathan Nolan teamed up with producer J.J. Abrams to deliver a hit series for CBS that ran for 103 episodes across five seasons. The series tackled topics like the increasingly intrusive nature of surveillance in the name of security and the rise of artificial intelligence, subjects that feel more relevant now than ever. The show is Person of Interest , and it's the ideal time for a reboot.
 'Person of Interest' Put a New Spin on the Standard Procedural
 Close Person of Interest CBS 
 CBS 
 USA Network 
 Debuting on CBS on Sept. 22, 2011, Person of Interest starred Jim Caviezel ( The Passion of the Christ ), Michael Emerson ( Lost ), Taraji P. Henson ( Hustle & Flow ), Kevin Chapman ( Rescue Me ), Amy Acker ( Angel ), and Sarah Shahi ( Red, White, and Royal Blue ). Nolan's series ran for five seasons and concluded on June 21, 2016.
 Person of Interest 's setup centers on a reclusive billionaire computer programmer, Harold Finch (Emerson), who built an advanced surveillance technology known simply as The Machine. It can collate all sources of information to predict terrorist acts and identify people planning them. The government uses the data it deems relevant for national security, while labeling ordinary criminal activity that is deemed " irrelevant ."
 Finch recruits a former CIA agent, John Reese (Caviezel), who the world believes to be dead, to be a field agent to prevent these murders, using a backdoor in the program that gives them the nine-digit Social Security numbers of people involved in these crimes. However, it is never clear whether the number reveals the perpetrator or the victim.
 Person of Interest was seemingly a standard CBS procedural with a sprinkle of sci-fi. However, Nolan used the formula of a network procedural like CSI to explore complex themes about security, preemptive criminal action, and AI. This made for compelling television in the 2010s, but it feels more necessary today.

 The Concerns Around a Surveillance State Have Increased
 Person of Interest CBS 
 Person of Interest was among numerous films and TV programs grappling with the debate between security versus privacy in the aftermath of 9/11, particularly due to the nature of the Patriot Act and the rise of surveillance technology. This is evident in popular media of the era, like Minority Report , 24 , and in the Nolan brothers' brief touch on it through sonar technology in The Dark Knight .
 Although the characters in Person of Interest use advanced surveillance technology to help people deemed expendable by those in power, the series constantly grapples with the ethics of its central premise. It questions whether predicting a crime before it happens is ethical, or whether making decisions based on data about an outcome that hasn't yet occurred inadvertently sets that outcome in motion. It highlights how little information they actually have to rely on, yet how much faith they put in The Machine.

 The idea of a surveillance state was already nerve-wracking in 2011. It is even more frightening in an era when facial-recognition technology is rapidly evolving. Such technologies being adopted by government agencies and businesses makes the ethical questions raised by Person of Interest even more pressing.
 'Person of Interest's Commentary on AI is More Topical Than Ever
 Close CBS 
 Person of Interest CBS 
 Person of Interest CBS 
 As Person of Interest continues, the AI aspect of the story comes into sharper focus . At the start of the series, The Machine can communicate only through a red light and provide limited information. Over the course of the show, The Machine and its competing artificial intelligence model, Samaritan, eventually become more complex and gain a form of consciousness. The Machine begins to speak through humans, showing how technology can overwhelm them.
 Since Person of Interest ended in 2016, surveillance technology and AI-powered tools have only grown. The results aren't always great, as overreliance on relatively new technology can produce false matches. In 2026, a report put out by the ACLU documented that more than a dozen people were " wrongfully arrested by U.S. police because of reliance on erroneous facial recognition results. "
 It's not just a security issue. AI has become a growing part of people's everyday lives , and it's getting increasingly bleak. From AI-generated videos that make it hard to tell what is real, to AI tools that replace certain jobs and leave many unemployed, concerns about the technology are no longer isolated to fiction.
 But beneath the higher-concept sci-fi plot devices, Person of Interest examines the value of human life and who gets to decide whose lives matter. The series kicks off because Harold Finch can't accept that those in power would let some die because they aren't deemed relevant enough in the grand scheme.
 Humanity's capacity for empathy, looking beyond cold data sheets and algorithms to make tough decisions, is what separates people from machines. The ability to see another person as more than a statistic or a probability is, in the end, what makes someone human. This discussion has come to the forefront in an age of algorithmic decision-making.
 How a 'Person of Interest' Reboot Could Work in 2026
 Close Person of Interest CBS 
 CBS 
 Person of Interest CBS 
 As with any television revival, the first question is whether the series should continue with its original cast and continuity or opt for a full-on reboot. Person of Interest completed its story after five seasons. Bringing back the original cast after all these years could provide an interesting change in direction, picking up with the characters after 10 years to see how they've changed with the world around them.
 Yet given how much the relationship to AI and surveillance has changed since Person of Interes t debuted, a new creative direction built from the ground up might be needed. The idea of an idealist computer programmer like Harold Finch might have felt appealing in 2011, but over the past 15 years, public sentiment toward tech billionaires as aspirational figures has shifted in the opposite direction. Just see the difference in both the stories of and reactions to 2010's The Social Network and 2026's The Social Reckoning .
 From the rising threat of AI to tackling the ethics of modern-day surveillance technology, A Person of Interest reboot would have plenty of new narrative avenues to explore. Even though Jonathan Nolan has his plate full with additional seasons of Fallout , maybe he will revive Person of Interest as a streaming series in the future. Alternatively, the show could be adapted as a feature film, similar to what happened with The Fugitive and Miami Vice .

 Personally, I miss the days when a television show was revived as a big-budget feature film. Movies like The Fugitive , Lost in Space , and Scooby-Doo felt special because they took a story from one medium and reimagined it for another, typically on a larger scale. Now it feels like every movie from Fatal Attraction to Cape Fear , and now Point Break , is being made into a television series. So if Person of Interest were to come back, I would like to see Jonathan Nolan direct a feature film adaptation.
